title: LightWM: Training-Free Hierarchical Working Memory for Small Language Model Agents
one_liner: Give a small agent a structured short-term memory so it can keep the facts needed for the current subtask without retraining the model.
lead: Small language-model agents are attractive because they are cheap to run locally, but they lose track of long tasks quickly. LightWM tries to fix that failure by storing task state in a structured memory system with one layer for the whole job and another for the current subgoal. The model is not retrained. Instead, a stronger offline writer prepares reusable memory templates because a fixed schema gives the small agent explicit slots to fill during execution.

problem.h2: Why long tasks break small agents
paras: A small agent often starts correctly and then drifts. After many actions, it forgets which room it searched, which object it already picked up, or what the current subgoal requires. When the remembered state is incomplete, later actions are based on stale facts.

Common fixes summarize the past in free-form text, but that summary can silently drop the one detail that matters next. LightWM argues that long-horizon performance improves when memory updates are structured around the task's subgoals, because the agent then reads and updates a compact state record instead of re-parsing a long history.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Prepare a reusable memory schema for each task family, then let the small agent update that schema at the task level and the subtask level as it acts.

panels.title: 1. Long history grows
panels.caption: Raw interaction history becomes harder for a small agent to use directly.

panels.title: 2. Summary drops a fact
panels.caption: Free-form summaries can lose a key detail because they compress many steps into a short paragraph.

panels.title: 3. Split the task into subgoals
panels.viz_args: find object -> open container -> place object
panels.caption: A task family gives a stable sequence of smaller jobs.

panels.title: 4. Keep two memory layers
panels.caption: Global memory stores whole-task state while local memory stores only what the current subgoal needs.

panels.title: 5. Choose the next action
panels.viz_args: small agent reads local memory and acts
panels.caption: Action selection becomes steadier because the relevant state is explicit.

steps.text: Use a stronger offline writer once to study how a task family is usually solved so that repeated steps can be turned into a reusable memory schema.
Turn those traces into slots for task-wide facts and subtask-specific facts.
Break the current job into subgoals that reuse the prepared schema.
Write new facts into the proper slots instead of extending a long free-form narrative.
Choose the next action using the compact state for the current subgoal.

paras: The paper changes how task state is represented during agent execution. Instead of storing the recent past as an unstructured note, it stores explicit fields for whole-task facts and current-subgoal facts.

hidden.name: Decision-relevant state retained at the current step
paras: The important hidden quantity is not how much history the agent has seen, but how much of the right state it still retains when choosing the next action. A short memory can work well when it keeps the facts that matter now.

LightWM tries to maximize retained useful state by separating persistent facts from temporary subgoal facts. That split matters because many details are needed only for the current subgoal, while others must survive across the whole episode.

heat.caption: Darker means the needed state is more likely to be missing or stale.

reads.html: What matters is whether the agent still has the right facts for the next move.
The method keeps decision-relevant state stable across long episodes by storing structured global and local memory updates.

paras: Structured memory helps because it turns recollection into slot filling. When the agent sees a new observation, it updates named fields such as current room, target object, completed subgoal, or missing prerequisite. That is easier for a small model to maintain than rewriting a long natural-language summary after every step.

The two-layer design also reduces distraction. The local memory for the current subgoal can stay short because it excludes older details that are irrelevant now, while the global memory still preserves facts that must survive across the whole task. This separation improves action selection because the model reads a smaller, cleaner state description at each step.

stages.s: map the task to a prepared subgoal schema
update task-wide and local memory fields
read local memory to pick the next action

math.words: At each step, the agent updates the task memory and the current-subgoal memory using the new observation, then chooses an action from the updated local state.
math.equation: global_t, local_t = update(global_t-1, local_t-1, observation_t, subgoal_t) ; action_t = policy(local_t)
symbols: the task-level memory after step t, holding facts that matter across the whole job
the subtask-level memory after step t, holding facts needed for the current subgoal
the new information seen at step t, such as room contents or tool status
the current smaller job inside the larger task
the structured memory writer that places new facts into the right slots
the action chooser that reads the local memory and picks the next step

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the task is: put the apple in the fridge.
At step 1, the observation says: you are in the kitchen, the apple is on the table, the fridge is closed.
global_1 stores kitchen, apple location, and fridge location because those matter across the whole task.
local_1 stores current subgoal = get the apple, target object = apple, blocker = none.
After the agent picks up the apple, local memory changes to current subgoal = open the fridge, carried object = apple.
The next action comes from local_2, so the agent opens the fridge instead of re-reading the whole history.

math.note: The paper's core point is that clean state updates can replace long free-form recall for procedure-heavy tasks.

items.html: If the offline writer builds the wrong slots for a task family, later updates will store facts in the wrong places, so the small agent will act on an incomplete state.
If the current subgoal is misidentified, the local memory will emphasize the wrong facts, because it is designed to keep only what matters for that subgoal.
A structured memory can still drift when observations are parsed incorrectly, because each bad update propagates into future action choices.
Use task families with repeatable procedures, validate the induced schema on a few held-out traces, and log every memory update so that failures can be traced to the exact slot that went wrong.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a household-task agent with three recurring task families such as fetch, open-and-place, and clean-and-store. For each family, prepare a simple global memory template and a local memory template. Then compare two versions of the same small agent: one that reads the full action history each step and one that reads only the structured memory.
The demo should show that the structured-memory version finishes longer tasks more often because it retains the right state for the current subgoal instead of relying on a long free-form recap.
demo.metric_eq: success_rate = completed_tasks / total_tasks ; memory_error_rate = wrong_or_missing_memory_fields / total_memory_updates
demo.closing: If success stays high late in the episode while memory errors stay low, the demo is capturing the paper's main mechanism.
